newsitem.title: INDIA: India celebrates republic in introspective mood.
newsitem.headline: India celebrates republic in introspective mood.

text.p: A brooding India celebrated its 47th anniversary as a republic on Sunday against a backdrop of sparring between political leaders and a sombre warning by the president against corruption and caste divisions.
At the nation's main parade in the capital, six MIG-27 jet fighters roared above rumbling tanks and colourful floats.
Other parades honouring the establishment of a socialist republic in 1950 and guarded by thousands of police and paramilitary troops were held in state capitals.
But the pageantry coincided with a bout of national soul-searching which has deepened with the approach of the 50th anniversary of independence from British rule on August 15.

"Lost Moorings", read a headline in the Asian Age. "Over the past 50 years, the country has lost its innocence, its idealism," the newspaper said in an editorial. "Even Mahatma Gandhi has now become the target of open vilification."

"Today, 47 years later, we seem to be sitting on the debris of the dreams of the founding fathers of our republic," Subhash Kashyap, former secretary of the lower house of parliament, the Lok Sabha, wrote in the Sunday Observer.

Corruption investigations against senior politicians, including former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao, and mounting tension between the ruling coalition and its diffident ally, the Congress party, have compounded the introspective mood.
"India's need today is for a profound moral and ethical rejuvenation," President Shankar Dayal Sharma said in a speech broadcast on nationwide television and radio on Saturday.
"There must be a forthright and outright rejection of casteism and communalism with its invidious, sinster nexus with corruption criminality."
State-run All India Radio broadcast a biting commentary by Karan Singh, veteran politician and scholar.

"The state of Indian polity cannot but be a source of concern to all thinking citizens," said Singh, son of the former maharaja of Kashmir, noting that the nation's fifth consecutive minority government was subject to much stress and strain.
"In society, divisive tendencies based on religion, caste and sub-caste are beginning to take their toll on our social fabric, and violence is becoming organised," he said.
Two percent annual population growth was placing a staggering burden on the second most populous nation, and widespread corruption was tarnishing the polity, he said.

"The moral and spiritual values on which our nation was based...are being rapidly eroded. Without this ideological underpinning, the whole concept of India as a powerful, moral force in world affairs has evaporated," he said.

Sunday's newspapers were covered with articles on a tit-for-tat battle between Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and Congress president Sitaram Kesri, whose party provides the centre-left goverment with crucial support in parliament.

Last week Deve Gowda failed to attend a reception hosted by Kesri to mark the breaking of the daily fast during the Moslem month of Ramadan. His absence was widely interpreted as reflecting mounting ill will between the two leaders.
Kesri, who has led efforts to reunify Congress following a humiliating defeat in general elections last year, shunned Deve Gowda's own "iftar" reception on Saturday night.

"At Daggers Drawn", The Hindu said. "Future historians may find it difficult to believe tha the fate of a central government came to be hinged on the prime minister's inability to find the time to attend an 'iftar' party."
